text:
4.9 References

OpenDP documentation: “Grouping” in the tabular-data tutorial, and “Aggregation” and “Polars” in the API user guide.
Korolova, Kenthapadi, Mishra and Ntoulas, “Releasing Search Queries and Clicks Privately” (2009): thresholded noisy counts as a way to release keys privately.
Desfontaines, Voss, Gipson and Mandayam, “Differentially Private Partition Selection” (2022): the threshold, its \(\delta\), and why one person’s groups add up.
The full edition’s chapters on sensitivity, whose stability-based release is the thresholded count, and on post-processing and composition, which is why a released key set can be reused for free.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.1 A privacy unit with an identifier
A survey respondent may own several rows, one per quarter. Earlier chapters used the fixed unit from The data and the context, allowing up to 36 rows per person and increasing every noise scale by that factor. This chapter uses PIDENT to identify a person’s rows and bounds their contribution separately for each query. The guarantee still protects the whole record, while the noise reflects the query’s contribution bound.
The chapter follows the documentation’s identifier-truncation page and user guide on truncation and bounds. It shows how to bound each person’s rows and groups under differential privacy (DP), and distinguishes bounds enforced by the library from bounds it trusts.
The script opendp_identifier_truncation.py runs every query on the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample with OpenDP 0.16.0. The scales, error bars, thresholds, error messages and facts about the data that it prints are the same on every run. The released values are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the page shows them in one block marked as one run.
Previously, the privacy unit was a number of rows. With an identifier, it is a column value. Datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours when one is obtained from the other by adding or removing every row with one PIDENT value. This is user-level privacy: it protects a person’s whole record, not just one row. The full edition’s chapter on user-level privacy defines and analyses it. OpenDP represents this unit with a metric on identifiers and distance one.
Here, contributions=1 counts identifiers rather than rows. In this survey, each person has at most one PIDENT value. The unit does not bound a person’s row count. The earlier bound of 36 had to hold across the entire dataset before querying; now each query specifies a bound that the library enforces through truncation.
The script first counts rows per identifier. This inspection is safe only because the data are public. For private data, derive the bound from the survey design; a bound calculated from the data leaks information.
The 36-row worst case is far above the observed maximum. An identifier spans at most four quarters but can own up to eight rows in one quarter.
The context follows the documentation and includes the public row-count bound from The data and the context. It splits an approximate-DP budget of \(\varepsilon=1\) and \(\delta=10^{-8}\) evenly across four queries. The quarterly table needs \(\delta\) because the library selects its keys from the data.
OpenDP rejects queries on this context unless they truncate, because it cannot otherwise bound one identifier’s effect on a statistic. In version 0.16.0, the error message does not identify the missing truncation.
The message blames the data scan rather than the missing truncation. On an identifier-based context, check that every statistic follows a truncation.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
print(dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT"))  # (SymmetricIdDistance { identifier: col("PIDENT") }, 1)


identifiers: 1,682,306  rows: 3,811,932
rows per identifier: p50=2 p90=4 p99=7 max=15
identifiers with more than 10 rows: 195
quarters per identifier: max 4  rows per identifier and quarter: max 8


def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, privacy_unit: tuple[dp.Metric, Any]) -> dp.Context:
    """The documentation's context: approximate differential privacy, split evenly over four queries."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=privacy_unit,  # dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT") below
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON, delta=DELTA),
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
        margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=MAX_LENGTH)],
    )
budget per query: epsilon=0.25 delta=2.5e-09

try:
    context.query().filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99).select(hours().dp.mean(HOURS)).summarize()
    untruncated = "accepted"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    untruncated = reason(err)
mean without truncation: A step in your query is not recognized at this time: "DF ["PIDENT", "YEAR", "QUARTER", "SEX", ...]; PROJECT */8 COLUMNS". ""If you would like to see this supported, please file an issue.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.2 Truncating each person’s rows
The documentation first computes the mean of HWUSUAL (usual hours), excluding code 99 (“not applicable”). The mean needs public bounds of 0 to 80 hours and a bound on rows per person. truncate_per_group(10) keeps at most ten random rows per identifier before aggregation.
mean_query = (
    context.query()
    .filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99)  # 99 means "not applicable"
    .truncate_per_group(ROWS_PER_IDENTIFIER)  # at most 10 rows per identifier, chosen at random
    .select(hours().dp.mean(HOURS))
)
mean_summary = mean_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
dp_mean = mean_query.release().collect().item()
mean, 10 rows per identifier: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=6,400.0 95% accuracy=19,173.2
mean, 10 rows per identifier: HWUSUAL Length, Integer Laplace, scale=80.0 95% accuracy=240.2
A mean uses a noisy sum and count, as in Essential statistics. They split the query’s budget share, so each gets \(\varepsilon/8\). Truncation limits count sensitivity to 10, giving scale \(10/(\varepsilon/8)\). Each row contributes at most 80 hours, so sum sensitivity and scale are 80 times larger. The full edition’s chapter on sensitivity derives how truncation and clipping affect sensitivity and the answer.
With a 36-row unit, the same mean has scales 23,040 and 288. Truncation can bias the mean by dropping rows after the tenth. Here it drops only 20 of about 1.5 million rows.
rows with HWUSUAL not 99: 1,496,192 by 809,710 identifiers
identifiers with more than 10 such rows: 18  rows dropped: 20
unit of 36 contributions, no identifier: scales 23,040.0, 288.0
The keep argument selects which rows remain. The default, "sample", retains ten random rows by shuffling each identifier’s rows and keeping the first ten positions. "first" and "last" follow file order; they are cheaper but can be biased when that order matters. SortBy retains rows ordered by an expression such as employment status, ILOSTAT. The scales are unchanged because each method retains at most ten rows.
truncate_per_group(10) plan: FILTER [(0.int_range([len().cast(Int64)]).shuffle().over([col("PIDENT")])) < (10)]
keep=first: scales 6,400.0, 80.0
keep=last: scales 6,400.0, 80.0
keep=SortBy(ILOSTAT): scales 6,400.0, 80.0
ILOSTAT values among them: [1]
Every retained row has ILOSTAT=1, so sorting makes no difference in this dataset.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
section: 5.3 Truncating the groups a person touches
text:
5.3 Truncating the groups a person touches
The second query groups responses by QUARTER and YEAR, releasing each quarter’s count and sum of hours. Noise depends on two bounds: rows one person can add to a group and the number of groups they can affect. Sensitivity is the product of these bounds. The full edition’s section on contribution bounding derives this result.
The query applies two truncations. truncate_per_group(1, by=quarterly) keeps one row per identifier and quarter; truncate_num_groups(10, by=quarterly) keeps at most ten quarters per identifier. Without the second truncation, OpenDP rejects the query and identifies the missing bound. The script omits the message’s suggestion because its column order changes between runs.
per quarter without truncate_num_groups: num_groups (None), total contributions (None), and per_group (Some(1)) are not sufficiently well-defined. This is likely due to a missing truncation earlier in the data pipeline.
The query follows the documentation but sets keep="first" for group truncation; the reason appears below.
quarter_query = (
    context.query()
    .filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99)
    .truncate_per_group(1, by=QUARTERLY)  # one row per identifier and quarter
    .truncate_num_groups(GROUPS_PER_IDENTIFIER, by=QUARTERLY, keep="first")  # at most 10 quarters each
    .group_by(QUARTERLY)
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True), hours().dp.sum(HOURS))
)
quarter_summary = quarter_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
quarters_hat = quarter_query.release().collect()
per quarter, 10 quarters per identifier: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=80.0 95% accuracy=240.2 threshold=1,714
per quarter, 10 quarters per identifier: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=6,400.0 95% accuracy=19,173.2
These scales match the mean’s: one row in each of ten quarters gives ten rows per person. Because the query has no public key list, OpenDP releases only quarters whose noisy counts exceed the threshold, as described in Grouping. Each quarter has at least 27,228 responses, so all 36 appear.
OpenDP 0.16.0 has two problems with truncate_num_groups. With the default keep="sample", summarize succeeds and release spends the budget share, but Polars fails during collect.
sample_query = grouped_query(context, keep="sample")  # the same table, with the default keep
sample_summary = sample_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
released = sample_query.release()  # spends the query's share of the budget
try:
    released.collect()
    sample_outcome = "collected"
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    sample_outcome = reason(err)
keep=sample: summarize scales 80.0, 6,400.0; collect: multiple fields with name 'QUARTER' found
shares spent after the failed collect: 4 of 4
The share is spent when the measurement is built. Polars can check the plan without reading data, so explain() detects the same error before release, at no cost. The toy frame demonstrates this check.
import opendp.prelude as dp
import polars as pl

dp.enable_features("contrib")
toy = pl.LazyFrame({"PIDENT": [7, 7, 7], "YEAR": [2005] * 3, "QUARTER": [1, 2, 3], "HWUSUAL": [35.0, 36.0, 37.0]})
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=toy,
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT"),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-8),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=100)],
)
quarterly = [pl.col("QUARTER"), pl.col("YEAR")]
query = context.query().truncate_per_group(1, by=quarterly).truncate_num_groups(10, by=quarterly)
query = query.group_by(quarterly).agg(dp.len(signed=True))
print(f"{query.summarize()['scale'].item():.1f}")  # 10.0
try:
    query.explain()
except pl.exceptions.DuplicateError as err:
    print(str(err).splitlines()[0])  # multiple fields with name 'QUARTER' found
keep="first" and keep="last" run, but their plans retain ranks below the requested group count. Polars ranks from one, so the truncation keeps one fewer group than requested, as the two numberings show.
import polars as pl

toy = pl.DataFrame({"PIDENT": [7, 7, 7], "YEAR": [2005] * 3, "QUARTER": [1, 2, 3]})
quarterly = [pl.col("QUARTER"), pl.col("YEAR")]
numbered = toy.with_columns(
    index=pl.int_range(pl.len()).over("PIDENT"),  # what truncate_per_group compares with k
    rank=pl.struct(quarterly).rank("dense").over("PIDENT"),  # what truncate_num_groups compares with k
)
print(numbered["index"].to_list(), numbered["rank"].to_list())  # [0, 1, 2] [1, 2, 3]
No identifier spans more than four quarters, so the script tests smaller values of k. Requesting four keeps at most three quarters and removes one quarter for each of the 13,948 identifiers with four. Requesting five keeps all four, with the scale and threshold for five groups.
truncate_num_groups(10, keep=first) plan: FILTER [(col("QUARTER").as_struct([col("YEAR")]).rank().over([col("PIDENT")])) < (10)]
identifier-quarters after the filter: 1,241,896  identifiers with 4 quarters: 13,948
truncate_num_groups(4, keep=first): keeps at most 3 quarters, 1,227,948 identifier-quarters; scale 32.0 threshold 657
truncate_num_groups(5, keep=first): keeps at most 4 quarters, 1,241,896 identifier-quarters; scale 40.0 threshold 830
In version 0.16.0, request one more group than you intend to retain and accept the corresponding larger noise. The guarantee remains valid because OpenDP calibrates to the requested count. The estimate can be biased because the dropped group is always last in sort order. The practitioner edition’s release workflow avoids this call.
Place truncations next to each other, with group truncation immediately before aggregation. A filter between them makes the truncation expression unrecognized.
a filter between the two truncations: Expr is not recognized at this time: dyn int: 0.int_range([len()]).shuffle().over([col("PIDENT"), col("QUARTER"), col("YEAR")]). If you would like to see this supported, please file an issue.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.4 One row per person
For a mean, grouping by identifier can be preferable to retaining ten rows per person. Aggregate each person’s rows to one row with a Polars expression, then take the private mean. After grouping, each identifier contributes one row.
person_query = (
    context.query()
    .filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99)
    .group_by("PIDENT")  # one row per identifier: the truncation
    .agg(pl.col("HWUSUAL").mean())  # any expression may summarize the person's rows
    .select(hours().dp.mean(HOURS))
)
person_summary = person_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
dp_person_mean = person_query.release().collect().item()
mean of one row per identifier: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=640.0 95% accuracy=1,917.8
mean of one row per identifier: HWUSUAL Length, Integer Laplace, scale=8.0 95% accuracy=24.5
Count sensitivity is now 1 and sum sensitivity is 80, so both scales are one-tenth of those with ten rows. No rows are dropped.
This changes the estimand. The first query averages responses, so a person with four responses contributes four times. This query averages person-level means, giving each person equal weight: 37.24 hours rather than 37.64. Casting to integers truncates each person’s mean toward zero and lowers the true value to 37.10. With an error bar of about 0.0035 hours, this choice matters far more than the noise.
true mean of one row per identifier: 37.0970  (before the cast to int: 37.2359; all rows: 37.6393)
per-identifier mean error bar at the true size: 0.0035

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.5 Bounds in the privacy unit
The unit can encode more detailed knowledge in a list of dp.polars.Bound objects. Each object specifies a grouping, the maximum identifiers per group and the maximum groups one person can affect. The documentation considers data merged from two sources that assigned identifiers separately. A person may then have two identifiers, increasing noise, but never two within the same quarter.
two_sources = dp.unit_of(
    contributions=[
        dp.polars.Bound(per_group=2),  # a person may appear under two identifiers
        dp.polars.Bound(by=QUARTERLY, per_group=1),  # but under one identifier in any quarter
    ],
    identifier="PIDENT",
)
bounded = make_context(frame, two_sources)
bounded_query = grouped_query(bounded, keep="first", k=5)  # each identifier may affect up to 5 quarters
bounded_summary = bounded_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
bounded_hat = bounded_query.release().collect()
two identifiers, one per quarter, 5 quarters: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=80.0 95% accuracy=240.2 threshold=1,714
two identifiers, one per quarter, 5 quarters: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=6,400.0 95% accuracy=19,173.2
one identifier as a bound, 5 quarters: scales 40.0, 3,200.0
The query keeps one row per identifier and quarter and up to five quarters per identifier. Two identifiers across five quarters give ten rows per person, so the scale is again 80. The second bound says the identifiers never occur in the same quarter; one person therefore adds at most one row per quarter. This does not lower count sensitivity because the ten rows may occupy ten different quarters. A single-identifier bound halves the scale.
num_groups can also bound the number of groups one person affects. The query then needs no truncate_num_groups, and a promise of ten quarters gives the same scale as truncating at ten. Unlike truncation, however, OpenDP does not enforce this bound. The script declares that no identifier spans more than three quarters, although the data contain 13,948 identifiers spanning four; the release proceeds without warning.
promised = dp.unit_of(
    contributions=[
        dp.polars.Bound(per_group=1),
        dp.polars.Bound(by=QUARTERLY, per_group=1, num_groups=3),  # a promise: at most 3 quarters each
    ],
    identifier="PIDENT",
)
promise_query = (
    make_context(frame, promised)
    .query()
    .filter(pl.col("HWUSUAL") != 99)
    .truncate_per_group(1, by=QUARTERLY)  # no truncate_num_groups: the unit already bounds the quarters
    .group_by(QUARTERLY)
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True), hours().dp.sum(HOURS))
)
promise_summary = promise_query.summarize(alpha=0.05)
promise_hat = promise_query.release().collect()
num_groups=10 promised in the unit: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=80.0 95% accuracy=240.2 threshold=1,714
num_groups=3 promised in the unit: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=24.0 95% accuracy=72.4 threshold=486
num_groups=3 promised in the unit: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=1,920.0 95% accuracy=5,752.3
identifiers that break the promise of 3 quarters: 13,948
The noise assumes three quarters, but 13,948 identifiers span four. Their privacy loss exceeds the declared \(\varepsilon\), with no warning in the output. Prefer truncation in the query, where OpenDP enforces the bound. Declare a unit bound only when truncation cannot express it, as when two identifiers represent one person and a filter cannot link them. Likewise, clip values in the query instead of declaring their range in the input domain. Assessing utility and choosing the noise revisits per-group bounds under Gaussian noise, whose scale depends on them differently.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds

5.6 The check against the truth
Because the data are public, the script computes each query’s value without noise. The first mean uses its own seeded sample of ten rows. For quarterly values, the check uses the first row per identifier and quarter, while the release selects a random row. The count check is exact; the hours check is approximate.

title: 5  Identifier truncation and bounds
text:
5.7 Summary



Table 5.1: The calls of identifier truncation and bounds, what each does, and the rule of thumb that goes with it.










Call or concept
What it does
Rule of thumb




dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT")
The privacy unit is every row of one identifier
contributions now counts identifiers; the rows per person are bounded by the query


A query with no truncation
Refused, with a message that blames the data scan
On a context with an identifier, every statistic sits behind a truncation


truncate_per_group(k, keep=...)
Keeps at most k rows per identifier, and per group with by
"sample" is unbiased; "first", "last" and SortBy are cheaper or deliberate, and biased when order matters


truncate_num_groups(k, by=...)
Keeps at most k groups per identifier
In 0.16.0, "sample" fails at collect after the budget is spent, and "first" keeps k - 1 groups; call explain() before release()


Truncations in a query
Must sit next to each other, the group truncation last
A filter between them makes the query unrecognized


group_by("PIDENT").agg(...) before a statistic
One row per person, so the sensitivity is that of one row
The best choice for a mean, if the mean over people is the one you want


dp.polars.Bound(by, per_group, num_groups) in unit_of
Finer bounds on identifiers per group and groups per person
A promise the library trusts; a person who breaks it loses more than \(\varepsilon\)


Truncate or declare
The query enforces a truncation; the unit declares a bound
Truncate, and declare only what no truncation can express

5.8 References

OpenDP documentation: “Identifier Truncation” in the tabular-data tutorial, and “Identifier Truncation and Bounds” in the Polars user guide.
Dwork, McSherry, Nissim and Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (2006): sensitivity and the Laplace mechanism.
Amin, Kulesza, Muñoz Medina and Vassilvitskii, “Bounding User Contributions: A Bias-Variance Trade-off in Differential Privacy” (2019): why truncating a person’s rows trades bias for variance.

The full edition’s chapters on sensitivity and user-level privacy derive the results this chapter states.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.1 Prepare inside the query
Survey data rarely arrive in the form a statistic requires. Work hours are floats, 99 means “not applicable,” and null means no answer. Response dates are split across two integer columns. Preparation may require casting, filling, clipping, filtering or recoding. This chapter shows where to perform those steps. OpenDP inspects the full lazy query and accounts for each step, so prepare data inside the query to keep that work within the guarantee.
The chapter follows the documentation’s tutorial on preparing microdata and its guides to data types and expressions. It describes the supported Polars contexts and expressions, OpenDP’s changes to them, and its treatment of nulls, undefined floats and bounds. The final example prepares Labour Force Survey (LFS) data to estimate the mean difference between actual and usual work hours.
The script opendp_preparing_microdata.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 with Polars 1.36.1. The noise scales, error bars, thresholds, error messages and true values that it prints are the same on every run. The released counts and mean are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so this page shows them in one block marked as one run.
A context on a Polars LazyFrame reads only its schema, which OpenDP treats as public, and accesses the data only at release. Before execution, OpenDP parses the query plan into a chain of transformations, as Transformations explains. It bounds each person’s effect at every step, so filters and fills in the plan are included in the accounting.
If you prepare data before creating the context, OpenDP sees only the prepared frame and guarantees privacy for that frame. A fixed row-wise function, such as renaming a column or parsing a date with a known format, preserves each person’s rows. The guarantee still applies, but you must justify that claim because OpenDP does not check the preparation. Data-dependent steps are unsafe: imputing with a column mean, bounding by its maximum or filtering at a quantile carries private information into the release outside the accounting. Before creating the context, use only public facts such as the schema, codebook and published sample-size bound.
The context uses the privacy unit and row-count bound from The data and the context: at most 36 rows per person. It splits an approximate differential privacy budget of \(\varepsilon=1\) and \(\delta=10^{-7}\) evenly over four queries.
At this point, the context knows only the schema and assumes that every column can contain nulls.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame) -> dp.Context:
    """The documentation's context: 36 rows per person, (epsilon = 1, delta = 1e-7) split evenly over 4 queries."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=EPSILON, delta=DELTA),
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
        margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=MAX_LENGTH)],  # public: a bound on the number of rows
    )
privacy unit: (SymmetricDistance(), 36)
privacy loss: (Approximate(MaxDivergence), (1.0, 1e-07))
budget per query: epsilon=0.25 delta=2.5e-08
schema: PIDENT=Int64  YEAR=Int64  QUARTER=Int64  SEX=Int64  AGE=Float64  HWUSUAL=Float64  HWACTUAL=Float64  ILOSTAT=Int64

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.2 Columns, filters and groups
Polars evaluates expressions in five contexts, which OpenDP divides into two groups. Expressions in .select and .agg may change row count or order, as aggregations do. Expressions in .with_columns, .filter and .group_by must operate row by row. This preserves the privacy unit: each person’s 36 input rows remain their own 36 output rows. Sorting or shifting could mix rows from different people, making one person’s effect impossible to bound.
The documentation first adds a column with .with_columns and groups by it. The row-wise cut expression bins usual hours at fixed breaks and replaces HWUSUAL with its bin. Because the labels depend only on the breaks, they are public keys.
def binned_counts(context: dp.Context) -> LazyFrameQuery:
    """How many responses fall in each band of usual hours: a row-by-row `cut`, then a count per bin."""
    labels = pl.Series("HWUSUAL", cut_labels(BREAKS, left_closed=True), dtype=pl.Categorical)
    return (
        lazy_query(context)
        .with_columns(pl.col("HWUSUAL").cut(breaks=BREAKS, left_closed=True))  # shadows HWUSUAL with its bin
        .group_by("HWUSUAL")
        .agg(dp.len(signed=True))
        .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame([labels]))  # the bin labels are public, so no threshold is needed
    )
binned counts: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 95% accuracy=431.9
without keys: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 threshold=2,973
true bins: null=20,819  [-inf, 0)=0  [0, 20)=89,495  [20, 40)=908,061  [40, 60)=406,947  [60, 80)=78,469  [80, 98)=13,220  [98, inf)=2,294,921
Scale is 36 rows per person divided by the query’s budget share. With public keys, every bin is released, including the empty bin below zero, whose signed count may be negative. Without public keys, OpenDP must determine from the data which bins exist, so it applies a threshold as described in Grouping. Null HWUSUAL values form a null bin absent from the key list and are not released. A margin on HWUSUAL also applies only to the original column, not the new bin column.
.filter removes rows using a boolean row-wise expression, such as the documentation’s filter for code 99 before a sum. A filter preserves most margin information but invalidates invariants about keys and group sizes. It also does not prove which values remain: a column filtered to non-null values is still nullable in its domain.
filtered sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=11,520.00 95% accuracy=34,511.3
The tutorial’s final context applies .group_by and .agg before private aggregation. In its sample-and-aggregate example, rows enter 1,000 groups by PIDENT, and the query releases the mean of each group’s minimum usual hours. The inner .agg accepts any expression, but privacy adds noise. The script compares mean scales under the current context and with a Bound from Identifier truncation and bounds that assigns each person’s rows to one group.
sample and aggregate: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=17,280.00
sample and aggregate: HWUSUAL Length, Integer Laplace, scale=576.00
one group per person: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=480.00
one group per person: HWUSUAL Length, Integer Laplace, scale=16.00
The first context does not use PIDENT to link a person’s rows, so it allows 36 changed groups. The inner aggregation doubles noise even with the bound: a changed group counts as one value removed and another added.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.3 The types OpenDP tracks
OpenDP assumes columns may contain nulls until an expression proves otherwise. It also tracks domain descriptors, facts about values that later aggregations need. Numeric descriptors include lower and upper bounds, set by .clip and removed by some later steps. OpenDP supports signed integers and unsigned 32- and 64-bit integers, but rejects UInt8. Float descriptors also record whether values may be NaN, an undefined numeric value; a float sum therefore needs both .fill_null and .fill_nan. Booleans and strings have no descriptors.
Categorical columns store integer codes and a label table. Two operations can make the table data-dependent. An expression such as .fill_null may add or remove categories, causing Polars to rewrite codes and emit a data-dependent warning. Also, codes follow the values’ order of first appearance, so grouping by them can reveal row order. OpenDP rejects both cases. An Enum fixes categories in the schema, avoiding these problems; cut is also safe because its encoding depends only on fixed breaks.
import polars as pl
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
status = ["working", "absent", "other"] * 100
unit, loss = dp.unit_of(contributions=1), dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-7)


def context_for(column: pl.Series) -> dp.Context:
    return dp.Context.compositor(data=pl.LazyFrame([column]), privacy_unit=unit, privacy_loss=loss, split_evenly_over=1)


categorical = context_for(pl.Series("status", status, dtype=pl.Categorical))
try:
    categorical.query().group_by("status").agg(dp.len(signed=True)).summarize()
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(err.message)  # Categories are data-dependent, which may reveal sensitive record ordering. Cast status to string before grouping.
enum = context_for(pl.Series("status", status, dtype=pl.Enum(["working", "absent", "other"])))
print(f"{enum.query().group_by('status').agg(dp.len(signed=True)).summarize()['scale'].item():.4f}")  # 1.0000
The error names the fix, a cast to string, and the enum query goes through. Dates, datetimes and times are also supported, with one time zone per datetime column.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.4 Casting, filling and clipping
The documentation recommends casting because floating-point sums incur rounding error. OpenDP accounts for that error, which can increase the noise scale for many rows and wide bounds. The script compares both sum types.
def hours_sum(context: dp.Context, as_integers: bool) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """The noise scale of a sum of usual hours, on the float column or after casting it to integers."""
    usual: Any = pl.col("HWUSUAL")  # typed Any: OpenDP adds the `.dp` namespace to expressions at run time
    column = usual.cast(int) if as_integers else usual
    return lazy_query(context).select(column.dp.sum(HOUR_BOUNDS)).summarize(alpha=0.05)
float sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Float Laplace, scale=14,405.18 95% accuracy=43,154.1
integer sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=14,400.00 95% accuracy=43,139.0
For integers, the scale is exactly 36 times the upper bound of 100 divided by the budget share; for floats it is slightly larger. Casting also changes error handling. Polars normally raises a data-dependent error when a value cannot be converted. OpenDP instead returns null, so every cast column is nullable and needs .fill_null before aggregation.
import polars as pl
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=pl.LazyFrame({"hours": ["40", "35", "n/a"] * 100}),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=1000)],
)
hours = pl.col("hours").cast(int)  # OpenDP turns "n/a" into a null instead of raising an error
try:
    context.query().select(hours.clip(0, 80).sum().dp.noise()).summarize()
except dp.OpenDPException as err:
    print(err.message)  # input data (hours) might contain nulls. Preprocess your data with `.fill_null`.
query = context.query().select(hours.fill_null(0).clip(0, 80).sum().dp.noise())
print(query.summarize()["scale"].item())  # 80.0
Earlier chapters’ .dp.sum handles imputation and clipping automatically. This snippet prepares the column manually and adds noise to a plain .sum, showing the checks OpenDP applies. A sum needs bounds from .clip; without them, one person’s effect is unbounded. .fill_null and .fill_nan remove bounds, so fill first and clip afterward. The script applies this sequence to the survey in .with_columns and tests incorrect orders.
def prepared_sum(context: dp.Context, steps: pl.Expr) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """A sum with noise on a column prepared in with_columns: OpenDP checks the steps left it non-null and bounded."""
    total: Any = pl.col("HWUSUAL").sum()
    return lazy_query(context).with_columns(steps).select(total.dp.noise()).summarize()
prepared sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=14,400.00
cast without fill_null: input data (HWUSUAL) might contain nulls. Preprocess your data with `.fill_null`.
clip before fill_null: input domain must consist of bounded data. Either specify bounds in the input domain or use make_clamp.
fill_null before fill_nan: input data (HWUSUAL) might contain nans. Preprocess your data with `.fill_nan`.
float prepared sum: HWUSUAL Sum, Float Laplace, scale=14,405.18
You can fill from another column, such as actual hours for missing usual hours. Both columns must be row-wise so their rows align, and the fill column must contain no nulls.
filled from a column: HWUSUAL Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=14,400.00
filled from a nullable column: fill expression must not be nullable
.drop_nulls and .drop_nans change column length by removing rows, so OpenDP forbids them in a row-wise context.
drop_nulls in with_columns: drop_nulls is not allowed in a row-by-row context
Recoding uses .replace or .replace_strict. .replace swaps selected values without changing the type. .replace_strict maps every value and may change the type; unmapped values receive default. The documentation says OpenDP sets a missing default to null, but version 0.16.0 does not. With three toy codes and a mapping for two, summarize succeeds but release fails. Always supply default to .replace_strict.
replace_strict without default: summarize scale=2.0; release: InvalidOperation(ErrString("incomplete mapping specified for `replace_strict`\n\nHint: Pass a `default` value to set unmapped values."))
replace_strict with default: released keys one other two

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.5 Predicates and arithmetic
OpenDP accepts Polars comparisons, conjunctions and arithmetic as row-wise expressions. Both operands of a binary operator must be row-wise, even in .select or .agg; otherwise a length mismatch could raise a data-dependent error. Tests such as is_null and is_nan are also row-wise and can define filters or grouping columns. The documentation counts respondents over retirement age by grouping on a comparison.
def over_retirement_age(context: dp.Context) -> LazyFrameQuery:
    """How many responses come from people over 64: a boolean expression as the grouping column."""
    return (
        lazy_query(context)
        .group_by(pl.col("AGE") > RETIREMENT_AGE)
        .agg(dp.len(signed=True))
        .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame({"AGE": [True, False]}))  # a null age is in neither group and is dropped
    )
over 64: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 95% accuracy=431.9
true over 64: true=1,190,845  false=2,620,832  null=255
Comparisons with nulls return null, so the 255 rows without an age form a third group omitted from the keys. One grouped query answers both sides of the comparison.
Version 0.16.0 does not support is_in, which tests membership in a list. Replace it with a disjunction of equality tests; the script uses this form to count employed respondents.
is_in: IsIn { nulls_equal: false } is not currently supported
employed: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 95% accuracy=431.9
The other is the absolute value, in Section 6.8.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.6 Strings and dates
OpenDP supports string parsing into temporal types through .str.strptime and its variants to_date, to_datetime and to_time. The format argument is required because inferring a format from data could make it depend on one person’s rows. OpenDP rejects nanosecond datetimes because the parser can panic on some inputs, producing a data-dependent error.
to_date without format: format must be specified; otherwise Polars will attempt to infer the format from the data, resulting in an unstable transformation
nanosecond datetime: Nanoseconds are not currently supported due to potential panics when parsing inputs. Please open an issue on the OpenDP repository if you would find this functionality useful. Otherwise, consider parsing into micro- or millisecond datetimes instead.
The survey stores dates in YEAR and QUARTER, not a date column. The documentation combines them with concat_str before the context because OpenDP rejects concatenation inside a query.
concat_str: Expr is not recognized at this time: ConcatHorizontal { delimiter: "-", ignore_nulls: false }. If you would like to see this supported, please file an issue.
Arithmetic is supported, so you can construct the date inside the query. Multiplying the year by 100 and adding three times the quarter gives an integer such as 200503. Parsing the string with %Y%m yields the first day of the quarter’s final month. .dt expressions then extract date components.
def quarter_end() -> pl.Expr:
    """The last month of the quarter as a date, built from YEAR and QUARTER and parsed with a fixed format."""
    year_month = pl.col("YEAR") * 100 + pl.col("QUARTER") * 3  # 2005 and 1 become 200503
    return year_month.cast(str).str.to_date(format="%Y%m")


def responses_per_month(context: dp.Context) -> LazyFrameQuery:
    """How many responses carry each quarter-end month, read off the parsed date."""
    return (
        lazy_query(context)
        .with_columns(DATE=quarter_end())
        .group_by(pl.col("DATE").dt.month().alias("MONTH"))
        .agg(dp.len(signed=True))
        .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame({"MONTH": pl.Series(QUARTER_END_MONTHS, dtype=pl.Int8)}))
    )
first dates: 2005 Q1 -> 2005-03-01  2005 Q2 -> 2005-06-01
per month: len Frame Length, Integer Laplace, scale=144.00 95% accuracy=431.9
true per month: 3=953,695  6=958,396  9=933,257  12=966,584
Each quarter ends in one of four public months, so the query uses those months as keys without a threshold. Their type is Int8, matching the output of .dt.month.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
section: 6.7 A worked preparation: hours lost to absence
text:
6.7 A worked preparation: hours lost to absence
The statistic is the mean difference between actual and usual hours for employed respondents. A negative mean means holidays, illness and short weeks outweigh overtime. The query performs each preparation step: it keeps ILOSTAT=1 (working for pay or profit), casts both hour columns to integers for integer noise (Section 6.4), fills missing usual hours with 0, then keeps rows with known usual hours, excluding 0 (variable hours) and 99 (not applicable).
Fill before filtering because a filter does not prove non-nullness to OpenDP (Section 6.2). The filtered column still has a nullable domain, and the next step uses it as a fill value, which must not be nullable. Missing actual hours are replaced by usual hours, making the difference zero. Finally, the query clips differences to the public range of ±40 hours, as required for a bounded sum. Using ±80 would double the noise.
def prepare[Frame: (LazyFrameQuery, pl.LazyFrame)](frame: Frame) -> Frame:
    """The rows of people who work, with their usual hours known, and the hours they lost that week, clipped."""
    low, high = LOST_BOUNDS
    return (
        frame.filter(pl.col("ILOSTAT") == 1)  # working for pay or profit
        .with_columns(pl.col("HWUSUAL").cast(int).fill_null(0), pl.col("HWACTUAL").cast(int))
        .filter((pl.col("HWUSUAL") > 0) & (pl.col("HWUSUAL") < 99))  # 0 is "varies", 99 "not applicable"
        .with_columns(pl.col("HWACTUAL").fill_null(pl.col("HWUSUAL")))  # unknown actual hours: assume the usual
        .with_columns(LOST=(pl.col("HWACTUAL") - pl.col("HWUSUAL")).clip(low, high))
    )
The function accepts a query or a plain LazyFrame, so the release and validation use the same preparation. The query ends with pl.col("LOST").dp.mean(LOST_BOUNDS); summarize reports its privacy cost.
hours lost: LOST Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=11,520.00 95% accuracy=34,511.3
hours lost: LOST Length, Integer Laplace, scale=288.00 95% accuracy=863.3
hours lost, bounds (-80, 80): LOST Sum, Integer Laplace, scale=23,040.00 95% accuracy=69,022.2
The mean uses a noisy sum and count, which split the query’s budget share. The sum’s scale is 36 rows times the bound of 40, divided by one-eighth of the budget. With bounds of ±80, its scale doubles. Clipping trades bias against noise: narrower bounds reduce noise but can increase bias. The full edition’s chapter on sensitivity derives the sum’s sensitivity.
Because the survey is public, the script measures clipping bias. On private data, use a public or historical copy for this check.
true prepared rows: 1,490,113  true sum of hours lost: -9,289,648  true mean: -6.2342
rows the clip changes: 42,830 (2.874%)  mean without the clip: -6.5319
mean error bar at 95%: 0.0268
Clipping changes fewer than 3% of rows but shifts the true mean from -6.53 to -6.23 hours, a bias of about one-third of an hour. This exceeds the noise. The script combines the sum and count accuracies into a mean error bar: the sum’s bar plus the mean times the count’s bar, divided by the count. The result is 0.027 hours. At this sample size, clipping bias, not noise, limits accuracy.
released (one run):
  bins: [-inf, 0)=-129  [0, 20)=89,491  [20, 40)=907,895  [40, 60)=406,594  [60, 80)=78,436  [80, 98)=13,452  [98, inf)=2,294,708
  over 64: true=1,190,894  false=2,620,771
  per month: 3=953,684  6=958,313  9=933,077  12=966,807
  hours lost: mean -6.2147  (true -6.2342, within 0.0268 with probability 0.95)
budget spent: 4 of 4 queries
Every count falls within its error bar of about 432. The empty bin is negative, which signed counts allow. The mean falls within its bar relative to the clipped truth. These four releases use all four budget shares. Assessing utility and choosing the noise develops the error-bar analysis further.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
section: 6.8 What a refused expression looks like
text:
6.8 What a refused expression looks like
An unsupported expression raises an OpenDPException with a variant and message when you build the query, before OpenDP reads any data. Absolute difference in hours is one example.
abs: Expr is not recognized at this time: [(col("HWACTUAL")) - (col("HWUSUAL"))].abs(). If you would like to see this supported, please file an issue.
The messages fall into two categories. “Not recognized at this time” means the expression has no implementation, as with concat_str and abs. Other messages identify a rule, such as a required format or non-null fill, and give the in-query fix. Rewrite unsupported expressions with supported operators when possible, as with is_in. Otherwise, apply the expression before the context only if it is a fixed row-wise function. Disclose this step with the release because OpenDP did not check it.

title: 6  Preparing microdata
text:
6.9 Summary



Table 6.1: The contexts and expressions of this chapter, what each does, and the rule of thumb that goes with it.










Call or concept
What it does
Rule of thumb




Preparation inside the query
OpenDP parses every step and accounts for it
Prepare before the context only with fixed row-by-row steps and public facts, and say so


.with_columns, .filter, .group_by
Row-by-row contexts: each person’s rows stay their own
A new column has no margins; a filter drops key and length invariants and proves nothing about what remains


.select, .agg
May change the number and order of rows
Binary operators and fills inside them still need row-by-row inputs


.cut(breaks)
Bins a number into categories with a data-independent encoding
Pass the labels as keys to avoid a threshold


Domain descriptors
Nullable, may be NaN, bounds

.cast

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
text:
7.1 What an accuracy statement means
Earlier chapters reported each query’s noise scale and accuracy before release. This chapter explains how to interpret and adjust them. Accuracy is an error bar’s half-width: with the stated probability, the released value is within that distance of the value to which noise was added. OpenDP converts between scale and accuracy, so you can price a target error bar before spending the budget.
The chapter also compares noise mechanisms. A pure differential privacy (DP) budget makes the context add Laplace noise; a zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) budget makes it add Gaussian noise. An argument to dp.loss_of selects the guarantee and mechanism. The choice matters most when one person contributes to many groups: Gaussian noise uses sensitivity proportional to the square root of the group count rather than the count itself. On the survey, this reduces quarterly-count noise six-fold under zCDP.
The script opendp_utility_and_noise.py runs every step on OpenDP 0.16.0 against the Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample of the earlier chapters. The conversions, scales, accuracies, thresholds and budgets that it prints are the same on every run. The released counts and the means of a small clamping experiment are not, because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so this page shows them in blocks marked as one run.
At a given scale, the released value lies within the error bar of the mechanism’s input with probability \(1-\alpha\), or confidence \((1-\alpha)\times100\%\). This book uses \(\alpha=0.05\), so about one in twenty releases falls outside the bar. Smaller \(\alpha\) gives a wider bar, as shown at \(\alpha=0.01\) in Essential statistics.
The opendp.accuracy module, exposed as dp in the prelude, provides eight conversion functions. Four convert continuous Laplace or Gaussian scales and accuracies; four functions prefixed discrete_ do the same for integer noise. The documentation’s example finds the Gaussian scale needed to stay within 2 of the input with 95% confidence.
The continuous conversions have closed forms. Laplace accuracy is scale times \(\ln(1/\alpha)\); Gaussian accuracy is scale times the two-sided normal quantile, about 1.96 at the usual confidence level. Discrete conversions sum integer-noise probabilities, so discrete Gaussian accuracy is an integer. Use discrete conversions for counts, which receive integer noise, and continuous conversions for sums and means of floats. At scale 180 the difference is small; summarize selects the appropriate conversion.
The error bar covers noise only. It measures the distance from the release to the mechanism’s input: the statistic after preparation. Clipping, imputation, row truncation and resizing can change that input. The bar does not cover the resulting bias relative to the intended quantity; repeated releases do not remove bias. The practitioner edition’s release workflow measures bias from truncation and clipping, which retain about half the revenue.

7.2 A target error bar on the survey
Suppose the survey response count must fall within 100 of its true value with 95% confidence. The count in Essential statistics used \(\varepsilon=1\) split among five queries. The excerpt summarizes that query and calculates the discrete Laplace scale required for the target accuracy.
laplace = laplace_context(frame, EPSILON)
count_laplace = laplace.query().select(dp.len(signed=True))
laplace_summary = count_laplace.summarize(alpha=ALPHA)
scale_needed = float(dp.accuracy_to_discrete_laplacian_scale(accuracy=TARGET, alpha=ALPHA))
epsilon_needed = CONTRIBUTIONS / scale_needed  # the Laplace scale is the sensitivity over epsilon
laplace count: Integer Laplace scale=180 95% accuracy=539.731
budget per query: epsilon=0.2000
error bar relative to the true count: 0.014%
discrete laplace scale for accuracy 100: 33.2152
epsilon that scale needs at sensitivity 36: 1.0838  (5.42 times the share)
The current scale, 180, is sensitivity 36 divided by the query share 0.2; see the privacy unit. Accuracy 100 requires scale 33.2, which would consume more than the full budget on this query. The current error bar is 0.014% of the true count, already small for a headline figure.
The conversion also gives the trade-off: Laplace scale is sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\), and accuracy is proportional to scale. Halving the error bar therefore doubles the budget. At \(\varepsilon=2\), this query’s scale is halved.
laplace count at epsilon 2: Integer Laplace scale=90 95% accuracy=270.115
The discrete conversion makes the bar slightly different from half because integer noise is rounded. The rule of thumb still holds. The full edition’s chapter on the Laplace mechanism derives the scale and tail bound.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
section: 7.3 Laplace under pure DP, Gaussian under zCDP
text:
7.3 Laplace under pure DP, Gaussian under zCDP
The budget type determines the default noise. dp.loss_of(epsilon=...) selects pure DP and Laplace noise; dp.loss_of(rho=...) selects zCDP and Gaussian noise. Other query details stay the same unless a query specifies a distribution, so the two context functions differ only in their budget declarations.
def laplace_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, epsilon: float) -> dp.Context:
    """Pure differential privacy: the context adds Laplace noise."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=epsilon),
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
    )


def gaussian_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, rho: float, delta: float | None = None) -> dp.Context:
    """Zero-concentrated differential privacy: the context adds Gaussian noise."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=rho, delta=delta),
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
    )
Privacy loss is the log ratio of an output’s probabilities with and without a person’s data. Pure DP bounds it by \(\varepsilon\) in the worst case. zCDP bounds its moment-generating behaviour: a mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when privacy loss has mean at most \(\rho\) and tails no heavier than a normal variable with variance \(2\rho\). The Gaussian mechanism satisfies this bound exactly, and \(\rho\) budgets add across queries like \(\varepsilon\) budgets. The full edition’s chapter on concentrated DP derives the guarantee. The documentation’s Gaussian example repeats the count with \(\rho=0.1\) split across five queries.
gaussian = gaussian_context(frame, RHO)
count_gaussian = gaussian.query().select(dp.len(signed=True))
gaussian_summary = count_gaussian.summarize(alpha=ALPHA)
privacy loss: (ZeroConcentratedDivergence, 0.1)
gaussian count: Integer Gaussian scale=180 95% accuracy=354
budget per query: rho=0.0200  sqrt(2 rho)=0.2000
continuous gaussian accuracy at scale 180: 352.7935
The scale is again 180. Let \(\sigma\) denote the Gaussian standard deviation (OpenDP’s scale) and \(\Delta\) the sensitivity. The mechanism satisfies \(\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\)-zCDP, so the context sets \(\sigma=\Delta/\sqrt{2\rho}\). At \(\rho=0.02\), the denominator is 0.2, matching the Laplace budget share. Gaussian noise has a narrower bar at equal scale because its tails decay faster. Equal scales do not imply equal privacy: Section 7.5 converts this \(\rho\) share to \(\varepsilon\approx1\), five times the Laplace share.
The Gaussian trade-off differs: scale is sensitivity divided by \(\sqrt{2\rho}\), so halving the error bar requires four times the \(\rho\) budget. The script confirms this at \(\rho=0.4\).
gaussian count at rho 0.4: Integer Gaussian scale=90 95% accuracy=177
Gaussian noise under zCDP offers no gain for a single count. Its advantage appears in queries that release many values at once.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
section: 7.4 One person in many groups: L1 against L2
text:
7.4 One person in many groups: L1 against L2
A grouped count returns one number per group. Noise is calibrated to the distance one person can move the full vector. Laplace noise uses the \(L_1\) norm, the sum of absolute changes; Gaussian noise uses the \(L_2\) norm, the square root of the sum of squared changes. Opposite corners of a unit square have distances 2 in \(L_1\) and \(\sqrt2\) in \(L_2\). In \(d\) dimensions, these distances are \(d\) and \(\sqrt d\).
Each survey respondent answers at most once per quarter, so their 36 records occupy 36 year-quarter groups, changing each count by one. The count vectors have \(L_1\) distance 36 and \(L_2\) distance \(\sqrt{36}=6\). Without this information, OpenDP must assume all 36 records fall in one group, making both distances 36. A dp.polars.Bound, described in Identifier truncation and bounds, supplies the per-group bound.
def bounded_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, privacy_loss: tuple[Measure, Any]) -> dp.Context:
    """A budget of either kind, with the privacy unit also bounded to one record per year and quarter."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(
            contributions=[
                dp.polars.Bound(by=[], per_group=CONTRIBUTIONS),  # at most 36 records overall
                dp.polars.Bound(by=["YEAR", "QUARTER"], per_group=1),  # and one in each year and quarter
            ]
        ),
        privacy_loss=privacy_loss,
        split_evenly_over=QUERIES,
    )
The query has no public keys, so its budget includes \(\delta\) and the context thresholds group counts as described in Grouping. The script summarizes quarterly counts under three settings: zCDP with only the 36-contribution bound, zCDP with a per-group bound, and pure DP with that bound.
bounded = bounded_context(frame, dp.loss_of(rho=RHO, delta=DELTA))
count_by_quarter = bounded.query().group_by("YEAR", "QUARTER").agg(dp.len(signed=True))
grouped_summary = count_by_quarter.summarize(alpha=ALPHA)
privacy loss with a threshold: (Approximate(ZeroConcentratedDivergence), (0.1, 1e-07))
grouped count, 36 contributions: Integer Gaussian scale=180 95% accuracy=354 threshold=1133
grouped count, 1 per year and quarter: Integer Gaussian scale=30 95% accuracy=60 threshold=184
grouped count, 1 per year and quarter, pure DP: Integer Laplace scale=180 95% accuracy=539.731 threshold=3712
true groups: 36  smallest 82,504  largest 131,656
The per-group bound reduces the Gaussian scale from 180 to 30, a factor of six, and lowers the threshold. Under pure DP it changes nothing because the \(L_1\) distance remains 36. Both thresholds are below the smallest quarterly count, so all groups are released; the Gaussian error bar is 60. The full edition’s chapter on the two mechanisms derives Gaussian calibration from \(L_2\) sensitivity.
When one person’s records are spread across many groups, \(L_2\) sensitivity can be much smaller than \(L_1\) sensitivity, making Gaussian noise under zCDP preferable. This gain requires a per-group bound. If public information cannot justify it, enforce the bound through truncation.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
text:
7.5 Stating the guarantee in epsilon
A \(\rho\) budget is convenient for accounting but less familiar to release readers. OpenDP converts it to \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) with two combinators described in Combinators. make_zCDP_to_approxDP produces an \(\varepsilon\)-versus-\(\delta\) privacy profile; make_fix_delta selects a \(\delta\) from that profile. The script applies them to a Gaussian measurement calibrated so sensitivity 1 costs exactly \(\rho\).
def epsilon_of_rho(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The epsilon that OpenDP's conversion gives for rho-zCDP at delta, read off a Gaussian measurement."""
    space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
    gaussian = dp.m.make_gaussian(*space, scale=1 / math.sqrt(2 * rho))  # sensitivity 1 at this scale is rho-zCDP
    approx = dp.c.make_fix_delta(dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(gaussian), delta)
    epsilon, _ = approx.map(1.0)
    return float(epsilon)
rho=0.1 at delta=1e-07: epsilon=2.3484
closed form rho + 2 sqrt(rho ln(1/delta)): 2.6391
rho=0.02 (one query) at delta=1e-07: epsilon=0.9951
the whole context converted: epsilon=2.3484 delta=1e-07
At \(\delta=10^{-7}\), the full \(\rho=0.1\) budget converts to \(\varepsilon=2.35\), and one query’s share converts to about \(\varepsilon=1\). The textbook conversion is \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho \ln(1/\delta)}, \tag{7.1}\] which gives 2.64 here. OpenDP’s tighter conversion over Rényi-divergence orders is derived in the full edition’s chapter on conversions. To convert a full context, apply the combinators to its accountant attribute, the measurement that composes all queries. It also gives 2.35, the value to report with the release.
You choose \(\delta\). Keep it far below the reciprocal of the number of people; otherwise, the guarantee permits a mechanism that publishes one person’s record. For 1.7 million people, \(10^{-7}\) is defensible. Conversion \(\delta\) is separate from the grouping-threshold \(\delta\), so a release using both must budget both.
The Gaussian count summary reports accuracy 354; the continuous conversion at the same scale gives 352.79. The context adds discrete Gaussian noise to integer counts, so it reports discrete accuracy, as Measurements explains. Use the discrete conversion to calculate count accuracy from scale.

title: 7  Assessing utility and choosing the noise
text:
7.6 Signed and unsigned counts
Every count here uses signed=True to avoid upward bias. Noise can make a small count negative; OpenDP previously clamped such results to zero. In version 0.16.0, signed=True casts the count to a signed integer before adding noise, so negative results remain. signed=False or an omitted argument clamps at zero; OpenDP warns that the default will change.
Clamping can reduce error for one small cell, but it biases sums of counts upward. A clamped count can exceed its true value but cannot fall below zero, so totals over many small cells accumulate positive bias. The OpenDP cookbook demonstrates this on 400 mostly empty cells: clamped totals are too high in every repetition, while signed totals are correct on average.
Clamp signed counts after release for display if needed; this is free post-processing. Release signed counts whenever others may sum, average or model them. The script illustrates the bias by releasing an empty frame 1,000 times with fixed Gaussian scale 30. It uses the framework API without a context and is intended only for toy data.
def mean_noisy_count_of_nobody(signed: bool, scale: float, repeats: int) -> float:
    """The mean of `repeats` noisy counts of an empty frame, at a fixed Gaussian scale, signed or clamped at zero."""
    empty = pl.LazyFrame(schema={"A": pl.Int32})
    domain = dp.with_margin(
        dp.lazyframe_domain([dp.series_domain("A", dp.atom_domain(T="i32"))]),
        dp.polars.Margin(by=[], max_length=1000),
    )
    count = dp.m.make_private_lazyframe(
        domain, dp.symmetric_distance(), dp.zero_concentrated_divergence(), empty.select(dp.len(signed=signed)), scale
    )
    return sum(int(count(empty).collect().item()) for _ in range(repeats)) / repeats
dp.len() without signed: warns=True clamped=True
expected clamped mean at scale 30: scale/sqrt(2 pi)=11.9683
standard error of the signed mean: scale/sqrt(1000)=0.9487
clamping experiment (one run): 1000 noisy counts of nobody at gaussian scale 30
  unsigned mean 11.48  signed mean 1.02  (true count 0)
The true count is zero. The signed mean is near zero and within the standard error of 1,000 draws. The unsigned mean is near 12, the expected positive half of Gaussian noise at scale 30. Repeated releases do not remove this bias; an unsigned table of empty cells carries the same upward bias in every cell.

title: The framework
text:
The Context API queries in the previous parts use OpenDP framework components. A private computation chains transformations and measurements. A transformation maps data to data, and its stability bounds how much the output changes when the input changes. A measurement maps data to a random release, and its privacy map bounds changes to the release distribution. These bounds propagate through a chain, while composed measurements accumulate privacy loss. This framework lets you inspect guarantees, build queries unavailable through the Context API and verify claims.
The first chapter defines domains, metrics, measures and the maps that describe stability and privacy. The next three cover transformations, measurements that add noise or select, and combinators for chaining and composition. The final chapter covers supporting utilities and shows how the Context API uses these components.



Table 1: The chapters of this part and the questions they answer.





Chapter
Question it answers




A framework to understand differential privacy
What are domains, metrics, measures, transformations and measurements, and what does each promise?


Transformations
How do I build and chain the data-to-data steps, and how does stability flow through them?


Measurements
Which mechanisms does OpenDP offer, and how do I calibrate each one?


Combinators
How do I compose measurements, convert between privacy measures, and account adaptively?


Utilities and the Context API inside
How do types, parameter search and serialization work, and what does a context do under the hood?






By the end of this part, you can build private queries from framework components, inspect guarantees with map and check, and describe how the Context API resolves a query.

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
8.1 Two kinds of object
The first two parts used the Context API to choose noise scales, spend budget and reject queries that exceed it. The framework beneath the context has two main objects. A transformation maps data to data and bounds how input distance affects output distance. A measurement maps data to a random release and bounds how input distance affects the output distributions. Each bound is a map from input distance to output distance; OpenDP uses these maps to track differential privacy (DP). This chapter shows how an object’s fields and map state its guarantee.
The script opendp_framework.py runs each example on OpenDP 0.16.0. Its sum example uses integer values from the Labour Force Survey (LFS) column HWUSUAL; its workflow uses the hundred toy scores from the first chapter. Domains, metrics, measures, maps, scales and error bars are deterministic. Released values vary because OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so the page labels them as one run.
The first chapter built a Laplace measurement with scale 1. The documentation repeats the construction at scale 5 using make_laplace, which takes the domain and metric as its first two arguments rather than attaching them with >>.
The constructor returns a Measurement; the script prints its fields.
Transformations and measurements share four fields. function holds the computation, which maps input_domain to output_domain; input_metric measures input distance. Their output fields differ because a transformation is deterministic and a measurement is random. A transformation returns data, so output_metric and the stability map describe its output distance as a function of input distance. A measurement returns a random draw, so output_measure and the privacy map describe the distance between output distributions.
The Laplace measurement accepts a finite float, measures input differences by absolute distance and compares output distributions by max divergence, bounded by \(\varepsilon\). Both object guarantees have the same form: a transformation is (d_in, d_out)-stable if inputs at most d_in apart produce outputs at most d_out apart; a measurement is (d_in, d_out)-differentially private if such inputs produce output distributions at most d_out apart.

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
def laplace_measurement(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    """Laplace noise of the given scale on one finite float, compared by absolute distance, under pure DP."""
    return dp.m.make_laplace(
        dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False),  # input domain: any float that is not NaN
        dp.absolute_distance(T=float),  # input metric: |a - b|, the units of the sensitivity
        scale=scale,
    )

laplace scale 5: input domain=AtomDomain(T=f64)
laplace scale 5: input metric=AbsoluteDistance(f64)

laplace scale 5: function=Function

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
8.2 Functions
Call a transformation or measurement like a function; invoke does the same. The clamp below clips each finite float in a vector to the interval [0, 5], under symmetric distance.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.symmetric_distance()
clamp = space >> dp.t.then_clamp(bounds=(0.0, 5.0))
print(type(clamp).__name__)  # Transformation
print(clamp([1.3, 7.8, -2.5, 7.0]))  # [1.3, 5.0, 0.0, 5.0]
print(clamp.invoke([10.0]))  # [5.0]
print(type(clamp.function).__name__)  # Function
The function field stores the computation as an object; the next part’s plugin chapter uses it to wrap a Python function. A transformation adds no noise and does not make its output private. It prepares data within the guarantee; only a measurement can release data. Printing a transformation’s output is outside that guarantee.
crumbs: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
8.3 Domains
A domain is a set of values. A map’s proof applies only to inputs in that domain, so the domain states its assumptions. When chaining objects, OpenDP checks that the first object’s output domain matches the next object’s input domain. The common atom_domain contains one value of type T; vector_domain lifts it to vectors.
import opendp.prelude as dp

floats = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)
print(floats)  # AtomDomain(T=f64)
print(floats.member(1.0), floats.member(float("nan")))  # True False
print(dp.atom_domain(T=float))  # AtomDomain(nan=true, T=f64)
small = dp.atom_domain(bounds=(-2, 2))
print(small)  # AtomDomain(bounds=[-2, 2], T=i32)
print(small.member(-2), small.member(3))  # True False
pairs = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=bool), size=2)
print(pairs)  # VectorDomain(AtomDomain(T=bool), size=2)
print(pairs.member([True, True]), pairs.member([True, True, True]))  # True False
member tests whether a value belongs to a domain. Type T uses Python names, so float prints as f64 and int as i32. The nan flag controls whether floats may be NaN; version 0.16.0 prints it only when true. Thus atom_domain(T=float) allows NaN, while atom_domain(T=float, nan=False) rejects it. A noise measurement needs the latter because absolute distance from NaN is undefined.
bounds restrict values to an interval. A sum needs bounds to have finite sensitivity. A vector domain can also specify size, which a mean needs, as the first chapter’s resize demonstrated.

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
8.4 Metrics
A metric defines distance between members of a domain. The framework uses it to interpret d_in; it does not compute the distance. Under symmetric distance, two datasets are separated by the number of additions and removals needed to transform one into the other, counting duplicates. The function below computes this distance for two small vectors from the documentation’s notebook.
from collections import Counter

import opendp.prelude as dp


def symmetric_distance(u: list[int], v: list[int]) -> int:
    """The number of additions and removals that turn the multiset u into v."""
    cu, cv = Counter(u), Counter(v)
    return sum(((cu - cv) + (cv - cu)).values())


print(symmetric_distance([12, 10, 8, 7], [10, 8, 7]))  # 1
print(symmetric_distance([12, 10, 8, 7], [10, 10, 8, 7]))  # 2
print(dp.symmetric_distance(), dp.absolute_distance(T=float))  # SymmetricDistance() AbsoluteDistance(f64)
print(dp.unit_of(contributions=1, ordered=True))  # (InsertDeleteDistance(), 1)
print(dp.unit_of(changes=1))  # (ChangeOneDistance(), 1)
Removing one record gives distance 1. Replacing 12 with 10 gives distance 2: one removal and one addition. Under symmetric distance, d_in is the maximum records one person can add or remove, which defines the privacy unit. Datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours when their input-metric distance is at most d_in. This is the metric behind dp.unit_of(contributions=k). In the LFS, one person contributes at most 36 rows (the privacy unit), so d_in=36.
Absolute distance is the absolute difference between two numbers. Under this metric, d_in is a sensitivity: the maximum change in an aggregate when one person’s records change. Sensitivity usually appears in the middle of a chain as an aggregate’s output distance, rather than as an input you specify. The full edition’s chapter on sensitivity derives common bounds.
Other dataset metrics modify symmetric distance. Insert-delete distance also protects record order. Change-one distance counts replacements in fixed-size datasets, the replace-one relation of bounded DP. Hamming distance is the ordered version of change-one.

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
8.5 Measures
A measure defines distance between probability distributions and gives a measurement’s d_out its privacy meaning. Max divergence is the largest log ratio between the probabilities of an output set under the two distributions. A bound of \(\varepsilon\) gives pure differential privacy, defined in the full edition’s chapter on the definition. OpenDP provides four measures, each with a different form for d_out.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
print(dp.max_divergence(), dp.zero_concentrated_divergence())  # MaxDivergence ZeroConcentratedDivergence
print(dp.smoothed_max_divergence(), dp.fixed_smoothed_max_divergence())  # SmoothedMaxDivergence Approximate(MaxDivergence)
space = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
gaussian = space >> dp.m.then_gaussian(scale=1.0)
print(gaussian.output_measure, gaussian.map(1.0))  # ZeroConcentratedDivergence 0.5
profile = dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(gaussian).map(1.0)
print(f"{profile.epsilon(delta=1e-7):.4f}")  # 5.6709
print(dp.c.make_fix_delta(dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(gaussian), delta=1e-7).map(1.0))  # (5.6708588354687715, 1e-07)
Under max divergence, d_out is \(\varepsilon\). Under zero-concentrated divergence, it is \(\rho\), the zCDP parameter that bounds a family of Rényi divergences and is the Gaussian mechanism’s native measure. At sensitivity 1 and scale 1, a Gaussian mechanism costs \(\rho=0.5\), equal to sensitivity squared divided by twice the scale squared.
The two smoothed measures express approximate DP, whose guarantee allows slack \(\delta\). Under smoothed max divergence, d_out is a privacy profile, a curve giving the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for each \(\delta\); the example evaluates it at \(10^{-7}\). Fixed smoothed max divergence, printed as Approximate(MaxDivergence), gives one \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) pair, as in the first chapter’s dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-7). make_fix_delta converts a profile to this pair. Combinators explains the conversions. Use output_measure to interpret a measurement’s d_out.
crumbs: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
text:
8.6 Stability maps and privacy maps
A map states the guarantee by converting input distance to output distance. For a measurement, map(d_in) returns the smallest provable d_out, so the measurement is (d_in, d_out)-differentially private. For a transformation, it returns the smallest d_out that makes it (d_in, d_out)-stable. check tests whether a proposed d_out meets the guarantee. The script evaluates a Laplace map at two sensitivities.
epsilon_at_1 = laplace.map(d_in=1.0)  # the sensitivity over the scale: 1 / 5
epsilon_at_10 = laplace.map(d_in=10.0)
fits = laplace.check(d_in=1.0, d_out=0.2)  # is map(1.0) <= 0.2?
too_tight = laplace.check(d_in=1.0, d_out=0.19)
laplace scale 5: map(1.0)=0.2 map(10.0)=2.0
laplace scale 5: check(1.0, 0.2)=True check(1.0, 0.19)=False
The Laplace privacy map divides sensitivity by scale. Sensitivity 1 at scale 5 costs \(\varepsilon=0.2\); ten times the sensitivity costs ten times more. Thus check passes at 0.2 and fails at 0.19. The Context API searches for a scale by testing whether check passes at the query’s budget share. The full edition derives the map in its chapter on the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms.
A map returns a provable upper bound, which may exceed the true value. The sum below illustrates this difference.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
float_sum = dp.t.make_sum(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0.0, 5.0))), dp.symmetric_distance())
int_sum = dp.t.make_sum(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(bounds=(0, 5))), dp.symmetric_distance())
print(float_sum([1.3, 3.8, 0.0, 5.0]))  # 10.1
print(float_sum.map(d_in=2))  # 10.00000004656613
print(int_sum.map(d_in=2))  # 10
print(int_sum.check(d_in=2, d_out=10), float_sum.check(d_in=2, d_out=10.0))  # True False
Two records bounded by 5 can change the sum by 10, and the integer sum’s map returns exactly 10. Floating-point addition rounds, so its proof includes a small extra margin. Because check uses strict comparison, the float sum fails at exactly 10. Use the map’s result rather than entering the theoretical value yourself.

title: 8  A framework to understand differential privacy
section: 8.7 Chaining a transformation and a measurement
text:
8.7 Chaining a transformation and a measurement
When a transformation’s output domain and metric match a measurement’s input domain and metric, >> chains them into a measurement. It applies the transformation first, then the measurement; the combined privacy map composes their maps. The script chains clamping, summation and Laplace noise for HWUSUAL, usual weekly hours. After removing nulls and code 99 (“not applicable”), the data contain 1,496,192 integer values from 0 to 80.
clamp = dp.t.make_clamp(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance(), bounds=HOURS_BOUNDS)
bounded_sum = dp.t.make_sum(clamp.output_domain, clamp.output_metric)  # the clamp's output space is its input space
laplace_int = dp.m.make_laplace(bounded_sum.output_domain, bounded_sum.output_metric, scale=LAPLACE_SCALE)
noisy_sum = clamp >> bounded_sum >> laplace_int  # the chain: its input space is the clamp's, its measure Laplace's
sum_sensitivity_1 = bounded_sum.map(d_in=1)  # one row of at most 80 hours
sum_sensitivity_36 = bounded_sum.map(d_in=CONTRIBUTIONS)  # 36 rows
epsilon_at_scale_5 = noisy_sum.map(d_in=CONTRIBUTIONS)
Each constructor uses the preceding object’s output space as its input, so domains match by construction. The clamp outputs integers from 0 to 80, which the sum accepts. The script prints the fields and maps along the chain.
clamp: input domain=VectorDomain(AtomDomain(T=i32))
clamp: output domain=VectorDomain(AtomDomain(bounds=[0, 80], T=i32))  map(36)=36
sum: output domain=AtomDomain(T=i32)  output metric=AbsoluteDistance(i32)
sum: map(1)=80 map(36)=2880
chain scale 5: input domain=VectorDomain(AtomDomain(T=i32))
chain scale 5: input metric=SymmetricDistance()  output measure=MaxDivergence
chain scale 5: map(36)=576.0
Read the maps from left to right. Clamping is 1-stable because it changes values without adding or removing records; 36 input records produce 36 output records. The sum changes by at most 80 hours per record, so 36 records give sensitivity 2,880. Laplace noise at scale 5 then gives \(\varepsilon=576\), an inadequate guarantee. The map exposes this problem before release; scale 5 was chosen for one float.
sum_scale = dp.binary_search_param(
    lambda scale: clamp >> bounded_sum >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale), d_in=CONTRIBUTIONS, d_out=EPSILON
)
noisy_sum = clamp >> bounded_sum >> dp.m.then_laplace(sum_scale)
sum_accuracy = dp.discrete_laplacian_scale_to_accuracy(scale=sum_scale, alpha=0.05)
released_sum = noisy_sum(hours)
chain for epsilon 1 at d_in 36: scale=2880.0 map(36)=1.0
chain for epsilon 1 at d_in 36: 95% accuracy=8,628.2 (0.01532% of the sum)
binary_search_param finds the smallest scale whose chained measurement passes check; here it returns 2,880, sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon=1\). The chain uses then_laplace, whose input space comes from the preceding object. The integer sum receives discrete Laplace noise and uses discrete accuracy. An error of about 8,600 hours is small relative to 56 million. Transformations and Measurements describe the other maps.
