title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.5 Nulls and the key set
Every table’s model requires a fixed key set for each column. As the documentation explains, keys come from keys, cuts or stable-key release; values outside the set become null before counting. Cut columns have no null key. Thus the four HWUSUAL bins cover its entire key set, although 20,819 real rows have unrecorded hours.
rows: 3,811,932  AGE nulls: 255  HWUSUAL nulls: 20,819
HWUSUAL = 99 (not applicable): 2,294,921
In version 0.16.0, nulls follow different paths. For a cut column, the one-way step joins counts to bin labels and omits null rows. The multi-way step assigns a null bin the last index, counting those rows in the bin above 40 hours. The resulting measurements disagree on the row total, so the fitted model compromises. The script compares its one-way HWUSUAL marginal with real counts that place nulls in the last bin.
aim model total (one run): 3,806,638.8  real rows 3,811,932
HWUSUAL bins (aim, one run): fitted count against the real count with nulls in the last bin
  (-inf, 1.0]: fitted 8,953  real 6,961  difference +1,992
  (1.0, 20.0]: fitted 121,660  real 119,893  difference +1,767
  (20.0, 40.0]: fitted 1,028,785  real 1,026,527  difference +2,258
  (40.0, inf]: fitted 2,647,240  real 2,658,551  difference -11,311
The last bin is eleven thousand rows short, while each other bin is about two thousand rows high. The model’s total, estimated from one-way marginals, is five thousand below the real count. The fit has spread the omitted null rows across bins.
The documentation’s remedy is to replace true nulls with keys before tabulation, using select or with_columns. The query’s fill option does this row by row without changing the privacy unit. The script maps null HWUSUAL values to 99, the survey’s code for not applicable, and 255 null AGE values to zero, the youngest bin. Choosing a replacement is a modelling decision, but both steps must assign every row to the same key.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.6 Guaranteeing marginals with Sequential
Adaptive selection may omit a marginal the release requires. Sequential runs algorithms in order on one table, each using the previous model. It divides the budget equally unless weights specifies another split. Placing Fixed before AIM guarantees the named marginals, while AIM uses the remaining budget where the model is inaccurate. The third release guarantees ILOSTAT by SEX and AGE pairs and fills the nulls.
sequential = dp.mbi.Sequential(
    algorithms=[
        dp.mbi.Fixed(queries=[dp.mbi.Count(by) for by in GUARANTEED]),  # these two marginals, whatever happens
        dp.mbi.AIM(rounds=ROUNDS),  # then AIM chooses the rest
    ],
)
sequential_query = table_query(context, sequential, fill=True)
table_seq, seconds_seq = timed_release(sequential_query)
sequential: rho per guaranteed marginal=0.0125  scale=227.6840
sequential: rho per AIM round=0.0025  scale of a round's marginal=536.6563
sequential release (one run): 12.1 s
sequential model total (one run): 3,811,712.7  real rows 3,811,932
sequential measured: ('SEX', 'ILOSTAT') std=227.68
sequential measured: ('AGE', 'ILOSTAT') std=227.68
sequential measured: ('SEX', 'HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=536.66
sequential measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'HWUSUAL') std=536.66
sequential measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'HWUSUAL') std=268.33
sequential measured: ('SEX', 'AGE', 'ILOSTAT') std=536.66
sequential measured: ('HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=536.66
sequential measured: ('HWUSUAL', 'ILOSTAT') std=536.66
sequential measured: ('SEX', 'HWUSUAL') std=536.66
sequential guaranteed marginals present: True
The one-way step again receives half the budget, and the remainder is divided equally between the two algorithms. Fixed splits its quarter between two marginals, each with scale 227.68. AIM uses the other quarter for ten rounds, so each marginal has more noise than in the first release: 536.66 rather than 379.47. This is the cost of the guarantee; weights can change the allocation. The model’s total is now 219 rows from truth, within one standard deviation of a one-way measurement, confirming that null handling caused the earlier discrepancy.
one-way SEX (sequential): tv=0.00004 largest cell error=240 rows  std=198.2 bound=0.00023
one-way AGE (sequential): tv=0.00006 largest cell error=233 rows  std=200.7 bound=0.00032
one-way HWUSUAL (sequential): tv=0.00009 largest cell error=273 rows  std=206.2 bound=0.00032

Every distance is at least three times below its bound, and no cell differs by more than 360 rows, less than two standard deviations. The largest HWUSUAL error fell from eleven thousand rows to 273.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.7 Generating the rows
ContingencyTable stores the Private-PGM model fitted in the previous chapter: a graphical model whose marginals jointly approximate the noisy measurements. synthesize() draws a frame from this model. It uses only released values, so repeated calls are post-processing and spend no additional budget.
synthesize (aim, one run): shape (3806638, 4)  model total 3,806,638.8  11.9 s
┌─────┬───────────┬──────────┬─────────┐
│ SEX ┆ AGE       ┆ HWUSUAL  ┆ ILOSTAT │
│ --- ┆ ---       ┆ ---      ┆ ---     │
│ i64 ┆ f64       ┆ f64      ┆ i64     │
╞═════╪═══════════╪══════════╪═════════╡
│ 1   ┆ 19.813324 ┆ 0.482324 ┆ 1       │
│ 1   ┆ 19.500078 ┆ 0.94265  ┆ 1       │
│ 1   ┆ 19.338927 ┆ 0.741979 ┆ 9       │
│ 1   ┆ 19.031755 ┆ 0.118982 ┆ 9       │
│ 1   ┆ 19.232563 ┆ 0.676039 ┆ 1       │
└─────┴───────────┴──────────┴─────────┘
synthetic AGE from 19.00 to 61.00  HWUSUAL from 0.00 to 41.00
synthetic dtypes: {'SEX': Int64, 'AGE': Float64, 'HWUSUAL': Float64, 'ILOSTAT': Int64}
synthetic SEX values: [1, 2]  ILOSTAT values: [1, 2, 3, 9]
Without rows, the frame size is the model’s noisy estimate of the row count. The columns retain their original types, and SEX and ILOSTAT use their key values. By default, method="round" scales expected counts to the requested row count and rounds randomly, so each synthetic marginal matches the model within one row per cell. method="sample" instead draws rows independently, adding sampling noise of about the square root of each count. Use it when rows should behave like a sample.
sample = table_aim.synthesize(rows=SAMPLE_ROWS, method="sample")  # draws rows independently from the model
synthesize rows=100,000 method=sample: shape (100000, 4)
The first rows have AGE just below 20 because the model stores bins, not original values. For cut columns, synthesize() draws uniformly within each bin and within one unit of the edge for open-ended bins. Synthetic ages therefore range from 19 to 61. Rows coded 99 receive hours just above 40.
The frame’s mean age reflects the bins and sampling rule, not the original data. Use finer cuts when numeric values matter, accepting more cells per marginal and more noise per cell (Evaluating and tuning synthetic data).
The script seeds NumPy’s global generator, used for rounding and within-bin draws. Thus the frame is deterministic given the released table.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.8 The privacy statement
The context has spent all three shares. The script builds the release statement from its variables.
budget spent: (0.3, 3e-07)
rho=0.3 at delta=1e-07: epsilon=4.2709
whole context converted: epsilon=4.2709 delta=4e-07
Report a \(\rho\) budget in \(\varepsilon\) using the conversion in Assessing utility and choosing the noise. make_zCDP_to_approxDP and make_fix_delta convert the budget of 0.3 to \(\varepsilon = 4.27\) with an additional \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\). Applying both combinators to the context’s accountant gives the same \(\varepsilon\) and total \(\delta\): three parts for key selection and one for conversion. The resulting \(\varepsilon = 4.27\) guarantee for the three adaptive releases is loose.
print(
    f"This release of three contingency tables and the synthetic rows drawn from them satisfies "
    f"(rho = {RHO:g}, delta = {DELTA:g})-zero-concentrated differential privacy, which is "
    f"(epsilon = {epsilon:.2f}, delta = {total_delta:g})-differential privacy, "
    f"for adding or removing all of one person's survey responses, at most {CONTRIBUTIONS} of them, "
    f"under the central model, using OpenDP {dp.__version__} with Gaussian noise. "
    f"The keys of SEX and the cuts of AGE and HWUSUAL were fixed in advance; the keys of ILOSTAT were released "
    f"with a threshold of {oneway_threshold}. Generating the rows is post-processing and spent nothing."
)
Post-processing extends the guarantee to the synthetic rows without increasing privacy loss. The statement also records which keys and cuts were public; choosing cuts from private data would leak information. The 36-contribution privacy unit inflates every scale by a factor of 36. Identifier truncation and bounds shows that few people contribute often, so the script builds—but does not release—the same query with an identifier unit and a four-row contribution bound.
context_id = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=frame,
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="PIDENT"),  # neighbours add or remove one person
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=RHO_QUERY, delta=DELTA_QUERY),
)
query_id = (
    context_id.query(rho=RHO_QUERY, delta=DELTA_QUERY)
    .truncate_per_group(TRUNCATE)  # at most 4 rows per person, so a person moves a count by at most 4
    .select(*COLUMNS)
    .contingency_table(keys=KEYS, cuts=CUTS, algorithm=dp.mbi.AIM(rounds=ROUNDS))
)
identifier unit, 4 rows per person: oneway scale=25.2982 threshold=142
identifier unit: scale ratio 9.00 = 36/4
The one-way scale falls nine-fold to 25.30 because each person can now change a count by at most 4 rows. The threshold falls from 1364 to 142, and all other release scales shrink by the same factor. This requires dropping every contribution after a person’s fourth row.

In the two releases without null filling, every marginal containing HWUSUAL exceeds its bound. Pairs without that column also have larger errors than in the third release because the incorrect total affects every marginal. After null filling, each measured marginal is at least four times below its bound. The bound assumes every cell is three standard deviations from truth at once, an unlikely event; a three-way distance near one thousandth therefore indicates a good fit.
This check does not assess unmeasured queries or models trained on synthetic rows. Evaluating and tuning synthetic data tests both and examines the effects of budget, cuts and rounds.

title: 17  Synthetic data with AIM and MST
text:
17.10 Summary



Table 17.1: The calls and concepts of synthetic data with AIM and MST, what each does, and the rule of thumb that goes with it.










Call or concept
What it does
Rule of thumb




dp.mbi.AIM(rounds=10)
One-way marginals, then rounds that measure the marginal the model fits worst
Fewer rounds for a quick release; read table.marginals to see what it chose


queries, measure_split, max_size
The candidates or a weighted workload; the share of a round spent measuring; the memory cap
The defaults serve a handful of columns


dp.mbi.MST()
One-way marginals, then pairs that form a spanning tree, measured at once
Faster than AIM when pairs are what matter; it never measures a triple


dp.mbi.Sequential(algorithms=[Fixed, AIM])
Runs the algorithms in turn on one table, splitting the budget evenly or by weights
Put the marginals you must have in Fixed; AIM spends the rest


query.oneway_scale, query.oneway_threshold
The one-way step’s noise scale and key threshold, before anything is spent
Under the identifier unit, 4 rows per person cost a ninth of 36


table.synthesize(rows, method)
Rows drawn from the fitted model; round matches its marginals, sample draws independently
Post-processing, so free; the row count defaults to the model’s noisy total


Cut columns in the synthetic frame
Values drawn uniformly inside the bin, within one unit of the edge for the open bins
Right as bins, wrong as numbers; give finer cuts if the numbers matter


Nulls in a cut column
Dropped by the one-way step and counted in the last bin by the multi-way step in 0.16.0
Fill them with a public code in with_columns before the table


Total variation distance against std
How far a synthetic marginal is from the real one, against three standard deviations per cell
A measured marginal over the bound points to the data, not the noise

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
text:
18.1 What good means
Synthetic data with AIM and MST produced a synthetic table and privacy statement. The statement describes privacy, not data quality. This chapter evaluates quality in three ways: compare measured marginals with the real data, test an unmeasured table, and train a classifier on synthetic rows and test it on real rows. It repeats these checks at three budgets and with MST, then lists what to publish with the data.
The documentation ends after generating rows. This chapter adds evaluation methods from the AIM paper and a benchmark of synthetic-data generators. The Labour Force Survey (LFS) sample is public, so it can be compared with its source. For private data, use a public or historical stand-in, never the data being protected.
The script opendp_evaluating_synthetic_data.py runs on OpenDP 0.16.0 and mbi 1.1.0, reusing functions from the previous chapter’s script. Budgets, scales, thresholds, conversions to \(\varepsilon\) and the classifier trained on real data are deterministic. OpenDP’s noise cannot be seeded, so releases, fitted models and distances vary; the page labels them as one run. Four releases took 55 seconds.
The benchmark by Tao and coauthors evaluates synthetic data with three questions. Do measured marginals match the real ones? Do unmeasured queries, such as a count over all four columns or a share in a small group, remain accurate? Does a model trained on synthetic rows work on real rows? Each test can reveal failures missed by the others.
Only measured marginals have release-based error bars. Their known Gaussian scales let the table’s std method estimate how far fitted counts may be from truth (Contingency tables). Unmeasured tables have no such bar, and neither do downstream models. Evaluate the second and third questions against real data. For private releases, use public or historical data of the same kind (the full edition’s chapter on public data).
The evaluation uses the previous chapter’s AIM release with nulls filled. It uses the same 36-contribution privacy unit (The data and the context), four columns, keys and cuts, and ten rounds. The budget is a privacy parameter \(\rho\) of 0.1 under zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), with Gaussian noise; a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\) pays for selecting ILOSTAT keys. Two functions build the context and query so later sections can vary the budget.
The first line releases the table. The next applies the same preparation to real rows: fill nulls, bin numeric values and map codes outside the keys to null. Thus real and synthetic marginals have identical cells.
The query and scales match the previous chapter: 227.68 for one-way marginals and 379.47 for each round’s marginal. At a further \(\delta\) of \(10^{-7}\), the budget converts to \(\varepsilon = 2.35\). In this run, AIM measured all four three-way marginals and then a pair at half the scale.
crumbs: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
text:
def make_context(frame: pl.LazyFrame, rho: float) -> dp.Context:
    """A context for one release at budget rho, with the previous chapter's unit and slack."""
    return dp.Context.compositor(
        data=frame,
        privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=CONTRIBUTIONS),  # neighbours add or remove one person's 36 rows
        privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=rho, delta=DELTA),  # zCDP with Gaussian noise; delta pays for ILOSTAT's keys
    )


def table_query(context: dp.Context, rho: float, algorithm: Algorithm) -> ContingencyTableQuery:
    """The previous chapter's query with its nulls filled, at the budget rho, with the algorithm plugged in."""
    return (
        context.query(rho=rho, delta=DELTA)
        .with_columns(synth.fill_nulls())  # every null lands in a public key before anything is counted
        .select(*COLUMNS)

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
text:
18.2 The workload error
The first test measures each released marginal’s distance from the real one. The AIM paper calls the workload-average distance the workload error, which AIM seeks to minimize. This is total variation distance: half the sum of absolute differences between cell shares. Equivalently, it is the largest share difference assigned to any set of cells. The worst distance below, 0.00102, bounds the share error for every query over those columns.
The function computes this distance for a list of cliques, the column sets covered by the marginals. It reads model counts with project_melted rather than drawing rows, which would add sampling noise (Section 18.6). It also reports the previous chapter’s bound: the distance if every marginal cell were three standard deviations from truth.
def marginal_errors(
    table: ContingencyTable, real: pl.DataFrame, cliques: Sequence[tuple[str, ...]]
) -> list[MarginalError]:
    """Each clique's distance between the fitted model's marginal and the real one, with the table's own standard
    deviation for it and the bound that three standard deviations in every cell would give."""
    errors: list[MarginalError] = []
    for clique in cliques:
        fitted = table.project_melted(clique)  # the model's counts: no rows are drawn
        tv, worst = distance(synth.marginal(real, clique), fitted, clique)
        std = table.std(clique)
        bound = synth.tv_bound(synth.cells(table, clique), std, real.height)
        errors.append(MarginalError(clique, tv, worst, std, bound))
    return errors

18.3 A query nobody measured
The second test concerns an unmeasured table. AIM considers marginals of at most three columns, so it never measures the 240-cell table over SEX, AGE, HWUSUAL and ILOSTAT. The model can still answer the query using a distribution that matches measured marginals and assumes no further relationships (the full edition’s chapter on query release). But the release provides no error bar for this answer.
try:
    four_std = f"{table_aim.std(COLUMNS):.1f}"
except ValueError as err:
    four_std = str(err)  # no measured marginal covers all four columns, so the table has no error bar for it

Here the four-way table is farther from truth than any measured marginal. Its error reflects noise in the measured triples and four-column dependence that no triple captures. The four measured triples overlap heavily, leaving little for the model to infer; therefore, the four-way distance stays near the worst measured distance. A release with fewer marginals relies more on model assumptions, as the MST results in Section 18.5 show.
Conditional shares are harder to estimate because they divide one count by another. From the four-way table, the script computes the employment share in 26 combinations of SEX, AGE band and HWUSUAL band with at least a thousand real rows. The largest error here is two percentage points for men under 20 who usually work 1 to 20 hours. All people in this cell work, but the model estimates a share of 97.95%. Noise is added to counts, not individuals, so small groups have larger relative errors. If analysts need small-group estimates, measure those groups, for example with Fixed inside Sequential.

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
section: 18.4 Train on synthetic, test on real
text:
18.4 Train on synthetic, test on real
The third test asks whether a model trained on synthetic rows performs on real rows, the benchmark’s “train on synthetic, test on real” task. The classifier predicts whether ILOSTAT equals 1 from SEX, AGE band and HWUSUAL band. It is a scikit-learn logistic regression with eleven indicator columns, one for each feature key.
The script draws 200,000 synthetic rows independently with method="sample". It also shuffles 400,000 real rows with a fixed seed. The first 200,000 train a real-data baseline; the remaining rows test both models.
rows = synth.synthesize(table, seed, rows=ROWS, method="sample")  # independent draws from the model
rows = synth.binned(rows.lazy(), table.keys, fill=False).collect()  # the numbers back in their bins
model = classifier(rows, table.keys, seed)  # train on synthetic
def classifier(train: pl.DataFrame, keys: dict[str, Any], seed: int) -> LogisticRegression:
    """A logistic regression that predicts ILOSTAT == 1 from SEX, the AGE band and the HWUSUAL band, fitted on
    `train`, which is either synthetic rows or real rows."""
    return LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=seed).fit(design(train, keys), labels(train))


def accuracy(model: LogisticRegression, test: pl.DataFrame, keys: dict[str, Any]) -> float:
    """The share of the held-out real rows the model labels correctly."""
    return float((model.predict(design(test, keys)) == labels(test)).mean())
held-out real rows: 200,000  real training rows: 200,000  synthetic training rows: 200,000
features: 11 indicators

train on synthetic (aim rho=0.1, one run), test on real: accuracy=0.9313  gap=+0.0000  mean probability difference=0.0015
The real-data model classifies 93.13% of held-out rows correctly, while 39.76% of those rows are working. In this run, the synthetic-data model has the same accuracy, so the gap is zero and well within the 0.0006 standard error. The test allows a one-percentage-point gap, which could result from errors in a few small cells.
Accuracy is coarse: models make identical predictions whenever each cell’s probability remains on the same side of one half. The script therefore also reports the models’ mean predicted-probability difference, 0.0015 in this run. For a single model, direct private fitting (Statistical modelling) is often preferable to training on synthetic data.

section: 18.5 What the budget and the algorithm buy
text:
18.5 What the budget and the algorithm buy
Tuning compares evaluation results across settings. The script runs AIM with one-fifth the budget, \(\rho = 0.02\), and five times the budget, \(\rho = 0.5\), then runs MST at the original budget. Each release has its own context because only one would be published. If all four used the same private data, they would compose to \(\rho = 0.72\). Tuning on private data therefore spends budget; tune on a public stand-in and release once.
mst_query = table_query(make_context(frame, RHO), RHO, dp.mbi.MST())
table_mst, seconds_mst = synth.timed_release(mst_query)
mst_eval = evaluate("mst rho=0.1", table_mst, seconds_mst, real, test_real, baseline, seed)

Larger budgets improve accuracy, but not uniformly. The worst measured marginal and four-way table improve across all three budgets, though less than the scales do. One-way marginals, already accurate at \(\rho = 0.1\), improve least. Share error falls most at the low end, from 15.64 to 2.05 points, because noise affects small groups first. With more budget, AIM also measures more marginals: four, five and six in this run. All four classifiers have accuracy 0.9313, so budget changes are not visible in this task.
The algorithm also matters. Here MST measures three pairs, each containing ILOSTAT. It therefore treats SEX, AGE and HWUSUAL as independent given employment status. This is false: among working people, hours depend on sex and age. As a result, MST’s four-way table is tens of times farther from truth than AIM’s at the same budget.
MST’s share error reaches 24 points for women under 20 who report at most one usual hour. Predicted probabilities differ by 0.028 on average, although accuracy is unchanged. Choose MST when pairwise queries suffice and release speed matters: it took 3.3 seconds, compared with 13.7 for AIM in this run.
The other settings are bin cuts and number of rounds. Finer cuts increase the number of cells in every marginal without changing noise scale, raising each marginal’s error bound. More rounds divide the budget into smaller shares, allowing AIM to measure more marginals at lower precision.

text:
18.6 How many rows, and how to draw them
The marginal evaluation reads the model rather than synthetic rows. Drawing a fixed number of independent rows adds sampling error to model error. The script estimates this error for each one-way marginal using the table’s shares, for both 200,000 rows and the real dataset’s size.

mst rho=0.1 pair ('AGE', 'HWUSUAL') tv (one run): model=0.01504  round=0.12370  sample=0.01261
With 200,000 sampled rows, SEX sampling error is many times larger than the model error in Table 18.1, so the sample is less accurate than the release. Sampling error still exceeds model error at the real dataset’s size because privacy noise at this budget is small relative to 3.8 million rows.
The default method="round" avoids sampling error; in this run, AIM’s rounded marginals match the model. In mbi 1.1.0, however, each column is drawn by a row’s rank within its parent-column group. Columns with the same parents are therefore sorted together and become dependent. In MST’s star, AGE and HWUSUAL share parents; rounding changes their marginal distance from 0.01504 to 0.12370, while sampling keeps it near the model. Use sampling when joint row distributions matter. If marginal accuracy matters, draw as many rows as the model’s total. Check pairwise marginals before trusting rounded rows.

title: 18  Evaluating and tuning synthetic data
text:
18.7 What to publish
A synthetic dataset needs a guarantee statement and enough information for users to judge what it supports. The practitioner edition’s chapter on release and governance gives the same guidance for trained models. The script supplies the numbers and identifies public information.
print(
    f"This synthetic dataset of {ROWS:,} rows was generated by AIM (OpenDP {dp.__version__}, mbi "
    f"{importlib.metadata.version('mbi')}, rounds={ROUNDS}, queries up to 3 columns) from one contingency table "
    f"over {', '.join(COLUMNS)} released under (rho = {RHO:g}, delta = {DELTA:g})-zero-concentrated differential "
    f"privacy, which is (epsilon = {epsilon:.2f}, delta = {2 * DELTA:g})-differential privacy, for adding or "
    f"removing all of one person's survey responses, at most {CONTRIBUTIONS} of them, under the central model. "
    f"The keys of SEX and the cuts of AGE and HWUSUAL were fixed in advance; nulls were recoded to "
    f"{synth.FILL}; the keys of ILOSTAT were released with a threshold of {aim_query.oneway_threshold}. "
    f"Drawing the rows by independent sampling is post-processing and spent nothing."
)
This synthetic dataset of 200,000 rows was generated by AIM (OpenDP 0.16.0, mbi 1.1.0, rounds=10, queries up to 3 columns) from one contingency table over SEX, AGE, HWUSUAL, ILOSTAT released under (rho = 0.1, delta = 1e-07)-zero-concentrated differential privacy, which is (epsilon = 2.35, delta = 2e-07)-differential privacy, for adding or removing all of one person's survey responses, at most 36 of them, under the central model. The keys of SEX and the cuts of AGE and HWUSUAL were fixed in advance; nulls were recoded to {'AGE': 0.0, 'HWUSUAL': 99.0}; the keys of ILOSTAT were released with a threshold of 1364. Drawing the rows by independent sampling is post-processing and spent nothing.
The statement covers the generated rows without an extra privacy cost because drawing from a released model is post-processing (the full edition’s chapter on properties). It covers this table only; other releases from the same people would compose with it.

The utility row is easy to mishandle. A distance computed from private data depends on that data; publishing it creates a release not covered by this statement. As Limitations and troubleshooting explains, the guarantee covers measured outputs, not separate computations. The std error bars are safe to publish. The distances here are safe only because the dataset is public.
This final chapter completes the workflow: release statistics, tables, models and synthetic rows through a context; evaluate quality on data you may inspect; and publish each release with a precise guarantee.
